Part 2: Your 15-minute talk

Chapter 5 of 45

Presentation guide: the oral examination

When and how long: Fri 13 Nov, 20 minutes. Test sharing on Teams and Zoom by 22 Nov.

Your 14 slides

The deck you share on Teams or Zoom. Slide 14 is a backup page of references. Open the PDF.

The exam: online, on Teams or Zoom, on a day the Program sets between 24 November and 2 December 2026 (Japan time). The guideline says: "Details of the oral examination will be notified on the day of the entrance examination." Prof. Zheng told you on 2 November to expect about 10 minutes on your work, 5 minutes on your research proposal, then about 15 minutes of questions. Most questions will be on your proposal, and some may be "Why Japan?" and "Why Hiroshima University?".

1. Files in this folder

File What it is
Sudhanshu_Pandit_Hiroshima_oral_exam.pdf Present this. 14 pages: 13 slides and one backup page of references.
Sudhanshu_Pandit_Hiroshima_oral_exam.pptx The same deck, editable, with the full script in the speaker notes.
FULL_SCRIPT.md What to say, word for word, with timings and the cuts for the 10- and 5-minute versions.
SLIDE_TEXT.md The words on each slide, and where each fact comes from.
old_meeting_deck_2_Nov/ The 6-slide deck from your meeting with Prof. Zheng. Do not use it in the exam.

The deck is built from /Users/mafex/code/personal/masters-research/2027-refresh/hiroshima-application/deck-oral/. To change a slide, edit build_deck.js there and run ./render.sh, then copy the new PDF and PPTX here. The speaker notes are read from FULL_SCRIPT.md, so edit the script first.

2. How to practise

You have about two weeks. Aim for three full run-throughs, each one recorded and timed, plus one test call.

First, read it aloud. Read FULL_SCRIPT.md out loud twice with the PDF open. Change any sentence that does not sound like you. Keep the facts and numbers the same.

Then record yourself. On your Mac:

  1. Open the PDF in Preview.
  2. Open QuickTime Player, then File > New Screen Recording. Under Options, choose your microphone.
  3. Present the whole talk to the screen, as if the panel were there. Do not stop if you make a mistake. Carry on, as you would in the exam.
  4. Watch the recording with the running totals from FULL_SCRIPT.md next to you.

Time it. Use a stopwatch. These are the checkpoints for the full version, counted from the moment your first slide is on screen:

When you reach You should be at about
Slide 4 (BrandMemory) 3:00
Slide 8 (start of the plan) 8:10
Slide 11 (the model) 11:00
Slide 13 (closing) 13:00
End 13:30

If you are more than one minute over, you are speaking too fast in some places and too slowly in others, or adding words. Look at where the extra time went.

Listen for these in the recording:

  • Speed. Calm and clear, about 115 to 120 words a minute. The panel are not native English speakers. Pause at each slide change.
  • "Like", "right?", "I would say", "basically". Your 2 November review noticed these. One or two are fine. Ten are not.
  • The numbers. Say each one clearly: "four hundred twenty-nine", "eight hundred twenty runs", "zero point four three".
  • The formula on slide 11. Say it slowly: "p squared, plus the variance of theta".

Three full run-throughs:

  1. Run 1 (by 15 Nov): alone, recorded, full version. Fix the sentences you stumbled on.
  2. Run 2 (by 19 Nov): alone, recorded, full version, then the 10-minute and the 5-minute versions once each.
  3. Run 3 (one or two days before the exam): with a friend on Teams or Zoom, with real screen sharing. Ask your friend to interrupt you once with a question, and once to say "please skip to your research plan". Then ask them three questions from 05_Questions_on_My_Proposal/.

Do not learn the script word for word. If you know what each slide is for, the cue line under each slide in FULL_SCRIPT.md is enough.

3. Screen sharing on Teams and on Zoom

Before the exam day (do this once, now):

  • As of 12 November, neither Teams nor Zoom is installed in /Applications on this Mac. Install both desktop apps from the official sites. The link you get will decide which one you use, and the desktop apps are more reliable than the browser.
  • Give both apps permission to share your screen: System Settings > Privacy & Security > Screen & System Audio Recording. Turn on Microsoft Teams and Zoom. Quit and reopen each app afterwards. Also check Camera and Microphone in the same place.
  • Do one test call on each app with a friend. Share the PDF, go through two slides, and ask the friend what they see.
  • PowerPoint and Keynote are not on this Mac. Present the PDF in Preview. It looks the same as the PPTX and needs nothing extra.

Set up the PDF:

  1. Open Sudhanshu_Pandit_Hiroshima_oral_exam.pdf in Preview.
  2. View > Single Page. Hide the sidebar.
  3. Plan A: share the whole screen with Preview in slideshow (View > Slideshow, or Shift+Command+F). Plan B: share only the Preview window, as a large normal window, not full screen. Test both in your test call and use the one that looks right on the other side. If window sharing shows a black screen, use Plan A.
  4. Turn on Do Not Disturb (Control Centre > Focus). Quit Slack, Mail, Messages, WhatsApp, Chrome tabs you do not need, and every AI app (see 12_Day_of/01_day_of_checklist.md).

On Teams:

  1. In the meeting, click Share in the top bar.
  2. Pick Screen (Plan A) or the Preview window (Plan B). Do not pick "PowerPoint Live".
  3. A coloured border shows what you are sharing. Ask: "Can you see my slides?"
  4. To stop: click Stop sharing in the bar at the top.

On Zoom:

  1. Click the green Share (Share Screen) button.
  2. Pick Screen or the Preview window, then Share.
  3. Zoom shows a green border around what you share. Ask: "Can you see my slides?"
  4. To stop: click the red Stop Share at the top.

Moving between slides in Preview: right arrow or Page Down for the next slide, left arrow to go back. In slideshow mode, Esc leaves the slideshow. To jump to a page, leave the slideshow and use Go > Go to Page (Option+Command+G).

Your notes: with one screen, the panel would see anything you put on it. Keep nothing else on the screen. The cue lines live in your head, and your printed research plan sits on the desk only if they say yes when you ask.

4. If you are cut off, or asked to skip ahead

"Please go to your research plan" or "Please skip ahead":

  • Say "Of course." Press the right arrow until you reach slide 8. From slide 1 that is seven presses. Say the bridge in one line while you go: "In short, every run reads the same rules file, so I want to measure how often runs fail together."
  • Then use the 5-minute cuts on slides 8 to 13.

"You have one minute left":

  • Go to slide 12. Say the two expected results in two sentences. Then slide 13: "I can build and run the agents. I want to learn to fit and test reliability models in this lab. Thank you."

A question in the middle of your talk:

  • Answer it briefly. Then: "May I continue with my presentation?" Go on from where you stopped. Do not start the slide again.

The connection drops:

  • Rejoin at once with the same link. If the video is slow, turn your camera off for a moment and keep the audio.
  • When you are back: "Sorry, I lost my connection. Shall I continue from slide 9?"
  • If your internet fails, switch to the phone hotspot (see the day-of checklist). If you cannot get back in within a few minutes, send the email in 12_Day_of/04_email_templates.md to the address in the exam notice.

Screen sharing fails:

  • Try once more: stop sharing, then share again.
  • If it fails a second time: "Sorry, my screen sharing is not working. May I present without slides? The plan is the same as in my research plan." Then use the cue lines in FULL_SCRIPT.md.

They ask you to stop sharing: stop at once and keep talking. They may want to see your face.

5. The shorter versions

The details in FULL_SCRIPT.md. In short:

  • Full (about 13:30 on the slides): the default. About 8 minutes on your work, 5:30 on your plan.
  • 10-minute (about 10:00): use it if they say "10 minutes" for the whole presentation. The plan stays whole. Your work gets shorter: one line for Magic Editor, no migration story, and short versions of slides 1, 2, 5 and 7. Lines marked [10 only] replace the long ones.
  • 5-minute (about 4:55): use it if they want only your plan, or 5 minutes in total. Slide 1 with the [5 only] line, then straight to slide 8, then slides 8 to 13 with the [cut in 5] lines left out. The numbers you skip are still on the screen.

If they give you a time you did not plan for, choose the next shorter version. Finishing early is fine. Running over is not.

6. How to point at the formula

Slide 11 has one formula: P(two runs both fail) = p² + Var θ(X), in the black box on the left.

  1. Say where it is first: "In the black box on the left..." The panel may see your slide smaller than you do.
  2. Move the mouse pointer slowly to the formula and hold it still for two or three seconds. In Teams and Zoom, viewers see your pointer when you share. In Preview's slideshow the pointer hides when it does not move, so move it a little to show it. Check this in your test call.
  3. Read the symbols in words: θ is "theta", ρ is "rho", p² is "p squared", Var is "the variance of", ≈ is "about". So: "Two runs both fail with probability p squared, plus the variance of theta."
  4. Then point at the picture on the right: "In both cases p is 0.2. On the left, both fail 4 percent of the time. On the right, 8 percent."
  5. Practise this one slide five times on its own. It is the slide where the panel will most likely stop you and ask a question.

If they ask you to explain without the slide, say: "If theta is the same for every input, the variance is zero, and two runs fail together with p squared, as if they were independent. If some inputs are harder, the variance is positive, and runs fail together more often."

7. What is not on the slides, on purpose

  • CV product numbers. The CV says Path AI "handles 1,500+ calls a month at 85%+ accuracy", Magic Editor was "used in 35+ customer workspaces in its first month", and BrandMemory "has built brand profiles for 75+ customer workspaces". None of these has a written source in your files, so they are not in the deck or the script. [CONFIRM: can you explain how each of these was measured? If a panel member reads your CV and asks, say only what you can explain, or "I am not sure how that number was measured, so I will not defend it."]
  • Your graduation month. Your CV and the proposal sent on 28 October say May 2026. Your official documents say July 2026, when the results came out. The deck says only "2026". [CONFIRM: if asked, say "I finished my final exams in May, and the university published the results in July 2026."]
  • Yuki for Mac. Its core is a fork of MacOS-Use. If asked about it, say so first. The deck shows only Yuki 2.0, which you wrote from scratch.
  • BrandMemory as a study. It was one A/B pair, one output on each side. The slide says so. Never call it a study.
  • The lab's N-version paper. You have read only the abstract. Never quote a number from it, and never say "I read your paper".

8. Likely follow-ups to each slide

Short, true answers. The full question bank is in 05_Questions_on_My_Proposal/ and 03_Mock_Interview/.

  • Slide 2, your paper: "It was a review and concept paper from my first year, with an assistant professor as first author. We had no dataset or model of our own. It taught me how to read and summarise research." Have the award certificate ready if you have it.
  • Slide 4, "What did you fix?": "I removed the per-feature limits of 3,200 characters and raised the overall limit from 6,000 to 30,000 characters. I turned off the default house style when a brand voice is active, and I moved the brand rules before the output requirements." Also true, if they ask what else you found: some rules that did arrive lost to a default house style that used strong words like "MANDATORY".
  • Slide 5, "How big was the test?": "45 replayed calls: 9 actions the user had not asked for, and 36 the user had asked for. It is small, and often one run per task."
  • Slide 6, "Do agents follow your rule?": "I have not measured it. That is part of why I want to do this research."
  • Slide 9, "Why not test compliance as an RQ?": "Compliance is only there to show that the change to the file worked. My question is about reliability."
  • Slide 10, "Why 10 runs?": "Ten lets me see how many runs fail on each input, within budget. The pilot will show whether it is enough."
  • Slide 11, "What if most inputs never fail?": "Then a zero-inflated beta-binomial may fit better. The pilot will show which one fits."
  • Slide 13, "Why this lab?": lead with the lab: "This lab measures how software fails with probability models, and my plan builds on your N-version study." Keep the personal reasons short.
